svg.title: OPFS persistence: the path this repo actually took, versus the one it didn't
svg.desc: Two real OPFS integration paths for the WASM demo: the async File System Access API on the main thread, which is what demo/persistence.go implements, versus the synchronous createSyncAccessHandle API, which requires moving the WASM binary into a dedicated Worker and was deliberately not built this pass. No throughput numbers are shown because none have been measured for either path in this repo.
svg.text: OPFS persistence: the path taken, not a benchmark
demo/persistence.go · no throughput numbers, because none have been measured

g.text: BUILT — async File System Access API
Runs on the main thread, same as the rest of the demo.
✓ FileSystemFileHandle.createWritable() / getFile()
✓ No Worker, no message-passing rewrite of the ~11
sopX() functions index.html already calls directly
✓ Real persistence: reload the tab, state comes back
✓ Tested end-to-end in headless Chrome via wasmbrowsertest,
not just built (demo/persistence_test.go)
✗ Not synchronous, not the near-native I/O path
navigator.storage.persist() requested at boot
best-effort; a browser can still decline it
NOT BUILT — createSyncAccessHandle
Requires moving the WASM binary into a dedicated Worker.
→ Only callable inside a dedicated Worker,
the Web platform enforces this, not a choice
→ Every sopX() call site in index.html becomes an
async postMessage / onmessage round trip
→ Real rearchitecture of a demo that already worked
and already had a recorded, tested walkthrough
＋ Would likely be faster: no data: URI / Blob
round trip for reads and writes
deferred deliberately, documented in
STRATEGIC_ARCHITECTURE_AND_MOAT.md §1.2

svg.text: This diagram states an architectural tradeoff. It is not a performance claim; no benchmark comparing these two paths exists in this repo.
